name: Ownership & moves
blurb: One owner per value, and what borrowing buys you

cards.title: Every value has one owner
cards.body: A `String` keeps its text on the heap and belongs to exactly one variable. When that owner goes out of scope, Rust frees the text for you — no garbage collector, no manual `free()`.
cards.tip: Owner leaves scope → value is dropped.

cards.title: Assignment moves
cards.body: Assigning a `String` to another variable moves it: the new variable becomes the owner and the old one can no longer be used. Pick what `t` gets and watch the compiler react.
cards.tip: `let t = s;` moves a `String`. Use `s.clone()` for a second copy, or `&s` to borrow.

opts.label: s
opts.note: The String moved into `t`, so `s` is no longer usable.

opts.label: s.clone()
opts.note: `clone()` copies the heap text: two owners, two Strings.

opts.label: &s
opts.note: `t` borrows the String; `s` still owns it.

cards.title: Copy types don't move
cards.body: Integers, `bool`, `char` and other small fixed-size types are `Copy`: assignment copies the bits, so both variables stay usable.
cards.tip: Only types that own heap data (like `String` and `Vec`) move on assignment.

cards.title: Borrowing with &
cards.body: A function that only needs to read a value can take a reference, `&String`. The caller passes `&s` and keeps ownership.
cards.tip: `&T` lends a value without giving it away.

cards.title: &mut is exclusive
cards.body: To change a borrowed value you need `&mut`. While a `&mut` borrow is in use, nothing else may touch the value — not even another `&mut`.
cards.tip: Many `&T` or one `&mut T` — never both at once.

opts.label: one &mut
opts.note: `r` is done before `println!` reads `v`, so this is fine.

opts.label: two &mut
opts.error: error[E0499]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable more than once at a time
opts.note: `a` is still in use when `b` borrows `v` again.
